speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: STATEMENTS AS TO PURCHASES BY UNITED KINGDOM IN CANADA IN 1950-51
speechtext:
In connection with my recent trip to the United Kingdom, I should like to
read into the record an agreed statement by the United Kingdom and Canadian governments recording the result of our wheat discussions.
"The Canadian Minister of Trade and Commerce held discussions in London with United Kingdom ministers on the subject of the United Kingdom's wheat requirements in the crop year 1950-51 within the framework of the international wheat agreement.
Both governments have now reviewed the results of those talks. They are agreed that the international wheat agreement removes the need for a contract to replace the existing Anglo-Canadian wheat agreement which expires at the end of July.
The United Kingdom government has made it clear that out of its total wheat import requirements in 1950-51, it expects to buy a large proportion in Canada which, quite apart from the special contractual arrangements for the past four years, is, and it is hoped will remain, the traditional source of supply for the United Kingdom. The Canadian government, for its part, is satisfied that Canadian wheat growers will continue to find in the United Kingdom a market for a very substantial part of their exportable wheat."
I should also mention that the United Kingdom has agreed to take 300,000 tons of Canadian flour at competitive North American prices as part of its purchases of Canadian wheat in the crop year 1950-51.
In the light of all our discussions, I think it reasonable to assume that in 1950-51 the United Kingdom will purchase from Canada between 100 and 120 million bushels of wheat. It is understood that such wheat will be offered upon international wheat agreement terms as to price, quality and position not less favourable than those obtained by any other buyer in the dollar market, whether in the United States or in Canada.

Perhaps I may answer a question which was asked by the hon. member for Souris on May 24 when I was absent from the house and was
brought to my attention yesterday. It reads as follows:
Will consideration be given to the request of the Canadian chamber of commerce that contributions to the Manitoba flood relief fund be exempted from taxation over and above the five per cent now allowed corporations and the ten per cent allowed individuals?
This question has come up before, more particularly with regard to the Fraser valley flood relief fund. As the hon. member is aware, these limitations of five per pent and ten per cent are fixed by the Income Tax Act. Any variation would require an amendment to the statute. On the previous occasion to which I have referred, it seemed that the only way in which an amendment could be effected would be to give the Minister of National Revenue discretion to exempt certain cases from those provisions. Aside from other considerations, it was felt that was placing an onerous responsibility on the Minister of National Revenue to differentiate between most desirable relief funds of this kind, and after careful consideration it was decided that it was neither desirable nor practicable to amend the Income Tax Act. The same considerations, of course, apply in this case.

subtopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO ORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENTS AND OTHER GOVERNMENT AGENCIES
PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO ORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENTS AND OTHER GOVERNMENT AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am merely speaking to clarify our stand on this resolution. When the leader of this group spoke on April 28 he stated that we were in general support of the amendment, the purpose of which was expressed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) on April 28, as recorded at page 1989 of Hansard, as follows:
What I have suggested would be the surest way of giving convincing evidence to the people of Canada that we have done all within our power to make democratic government in this country as efficient and as economical as is humanly possible.
In view of the fact that it is a month now since this resolution was moved, I will quote the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition, which is as follows:
"Consideration should be given to the matter of appointing a royal commission for the purpose of examining and making recommendations for:
1.	Reducing public expenditure to the lowest point consistent with efficiency.
2.	Eliminating duplication of overlapping services.
3.	Consolidating all public services and departmental activities of a similar nature.
4.	Improving the general efficiency of government and assuring to all members of the civil service full recognition of their responsibilities.
And without limiting the generality of the foregoing to make such further recommendations as may contribute to the general efficiency of the organization of government."
The leader of this group made it quite clear that we would not support any program of cheese-paring or curtailing of essential services. But on the other hand we do believe that economies can be effected in the cost of administration.
However, section 1 of this resolution is open to many interpretations, and may mean far more than the establishment of economical administration. It may very well mean a general curtailment of public expenditures. For instance, section 1 places the main emphasis on the reduction of public expenditures; but if public expenditures are to be at a level consistent with efficiency, it may well mean that they will have to be increased rather than reduced. We feel that the amendment should have read, "to control public expenditures at a level that will be consistent with efficiency."

The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell) took issue with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) for saying that expenditures could not be reduced below the level of $2,400 million. Evidently the hon. member for Greenwood felt that expenditures could be reduced below that level by establishing economies and also by eliminating wasteful expenditures. On the other hand there is need to expand expenditures of some of the departments of government. Therefore in the over-all picture you might very well have an expansion of government expenditures rather than a reduction through the reducing of administration costs.
It seems to us that the main point is to control public expenditures at a level that will provide for most efficient operation and servicing of the Canadian economy. Toward that end members of all parties in this house have from time to time urged an increase in certain government expenditures. For instance, recently we had a debate on the question of government grants to the provinces for educati n. Members from all parties urged an increase in expenditures for that purpose. We have also had debates on irrigation. Members of all parties have urged the federal government to increase their expenditures on irrigation. There has also been a great deal of discussion in the house about water conservation, flood control and reforestation. At the present time we have before us the picture of Winnipeg. We realize how necessary it is to establish flood control measures. There is an old Chinese saying to the effect that to control the rivers you must also control the hills. Of course in controlling the hills you will require to adopt a program of reforestation and building of reservoirs. As I say, members, on both sides of the house have repeatedly urged an increase in expenditures for that purpose.
Last session we had a discussion about the federal share of financing the trans-Canada highway. Members on all sides emphasized the fact that the federal government should take the larger share in that financial responsibility. All these expenditures may be considered to be self-liquidating, but they would mean a substantial increase in government expenditures at this time.
All parties in the house have urged an increase in government expenditures for social services, especially for old age pensions. All parties have urged an increase in the amount of war veterans allowance from $40 to $50 a month. Members of various parties have urged the necessity of maintaining a substantial floor under agricultural prices and for the purpose of mking a substantial payment on the five year wheat pool. These payments would no doubt be greater than the

reductions by the elimination of waste or by making cuts in the cost of administration. Therefore, for that reason, I am not prepared to support the motion to reduce public expenditures when it may very well be in the interests of Canada to increase public expenditures in the future.
The Conservative party emphasizes the need to expand production in order to ease the burden of debt and taxation, and I would agree with that wholeheartedly. I think members on both sides of the house would agree with the necessity of doing that very thing; but let us not forget for one minute that a prerequisite of increased production is an effective demand against that production, which means increased spending by the people of Canada. Some hon. members may say, not necessarily an increase in spending by the people of Canada; it may mean an increase in exports. But an increase in exports must mean also an increase in imports, and an increase in imports means an increase in sales internally. That means an increase in spending by the Canadian people. Therefore before you can hope to get industries to expand greatly their production, you must be in a position to assure them that when they expand that production they will be able to sell it.
I found it most refreshing to read a copy of a speech made by the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) before the advertising and sales club at Toronto on April 14, 1950. Since this is a new type of speech to come from a member of this government, I am going to quote a number of passages from it. I will say in advance that I concur in everything that he said in that speech. He was referring to the problems of the fifties, and he said:
Most of our factories are in tip-top shape. Our workers are experienced and skilled. Our farms are well mechanized. Thanks to hard work and widespread ability the supply problems of the forties have been well-nigh licked.
Looking to the fifties, the problem is: will there be sufficient demand both at home and abroad for the things our heavily industrialized economy can produce? One way of finding out how big the demand really is, is to sell, sell, and sell again. For remember the economic repercussions of what might happen if you sell less than you used to.
Then he went on:
Canada's prosperity in the fifties will depend not only on your ability to sell. It will also depend, among other things, on the willingness of Canadian consumers to buy. And here a major responsibility rests on the shoulders of Canadian women.
Under the heading: "Canadian Women-A major factor in maintaining sales", he had this to say:
Now what I have to say may appeal to the ladies, though I am not so sure about the reaction of some of the husbands. If Canadian consumers-and that
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry
includes the ladies here and their sisters in every part of our country.-don't keep on buying, sales people will sell less, producers will produce less, and there will be less employment and less income. In the end there will be less of everything.
Referring to the high level of consumption essential to prosperity, he said this:
In putting great emphasis on the point that consumers should spend, salesmen should sell and producers should produce, I am not unmindful of the fact that Canadians also want to put something away for a rainy day. I agree that this is important. But for the nation as a whole a situation may arise where there is too much of a good thing. If all Canadians were to try to save too much, less would be spent on consumer goods and services. And if less money is spent on consumer goods, businessmen will have little incentive to expand capital facilities. And if there is a decline in private investment, not only will many private savings remain unused-in the absence of the government's taking a hand in the matter-but men will be laid off work in capital goods industries. And off we will be on the road toward a depression.
The major domestic challenge of the fifties, then, will be whether consumers can be persuaded to keep on buying, and how effective sales and advertising efforts based on increasingly efficient production will be in keeping up sales.
He concluded with these words:
To put it into nine simple words: buy more, enjoy more, and Canada will remain prosperous.
That is a happy slogan. I would remind the house that it is the type of speech that we in this group were making in the thirties, every time we stressed the fact that increased saving on the part of the people, while highly desirable from the point of view of the individual, might have a detrimental effect on the economy of the country by bringing about a reduction in spending, unsold goods, and an increase in unemployment. I am sorry the Minister of Resources and Development did not go one step further. He told the people what would happen if they continued to save at their present rate, and if sales declined. He did not say, however, what the government was prepared to do.
In other words, if the people of Canada do not take his advice and do not step up their spending, is the federal government going to sit idly by and see a depression develop, as he forecast in his speech would be the case unless the people increased their spending? If unemployment becomes a problem, and if private spending fails to create effective demand, which would cause surpluses of goods, curtailed production and expanding unemployment, then we say the government would be justified in expanding expenditures without meeting the full cost by taxation or by borrowing the savings of the people.
It is very interesting to note that the governor of the Bank of Canada, speaking on that very point back in 1943, agreed that if such a situation developed as was envisaged

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry by the Minister of Resources and Development, the government would be justified in expanding its expenditures without meeting the full cost from taxation or borrowing from the savings of the people.
In this connection I quote from a broadcast entitled "The Shape of Things To Come," which went out on April 4, 1943, and in which Mr. Graham Towers and I participated. At that time we discussed the subject of post-war financing, and the discussion ensued in this way:

speechtext:
After the war the need will be to
encourage private spending. Heavy taxes and public borrowing will be contrary to the public welfare. Will the government finance all desirable public projects by credit expansion when necessary?

subtopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO ORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENTS AND OTHER GOVERNMENT AGENCIES
speechtext:
In circumstances such as Mr. Quelch describes, I would say that there would be grounds for government not meeting the entire cost of its programs by taxing and drawing on public savings. The desire would be to encourage private spending and make government investment more of a residual item. If part of the necessary money had to come from credit expansion.-and the projects were sound and in the public interest-then I should say, go ahead.
So when the Minister of Resources and Development warns the Canadian people that unless they increase their spending we will have a depression, I should like him also to say that if the people do not take that advice and if a depression does develop, the federal government will be prepared to step in and take up the slack as recommended by Mr. Graham Towers in the broadcast to which I have referred.
We believe that the royal commission which is urged by the amendment might well recommend setting up a commission similar to that set up in the United States back in 1934, to make a survey of the potential productive capacity of the country, with special reference to the relationship between national production and national income, so as to find out. to what extent demand lags behind supply. It could then make a recommendation to the government as to steps which might be taken to ensure that there would be effective demand for the production of the country.
If the government can give business in Canada the assurance that demand will be maintained at all times, I am satisfied that industry in this country will at all times have sufficient confidence to go ahead and expand production. Therefore, as public expenditures should be controlled in this country at a level required to help provide a balanced economy-and by that I mean a condition under which production is maintained at the optimum level and at the same time effective

demand maintained' against that-I move, seconded by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Wylie):
That the amendment be amended by striking out clause 1 and substituting therefor the following:
I.	Controlling public expenditure at a level consistent with efficiency.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not originally planned to speak in this debate, until I heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) say how very easy it was for members of the apposition to obtain, information in answer to questions. He began to enumerate members of the opposition, and pointed out that there was one in particular, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), who did know how to ask questions and how to obtain information.
During the last few days when the orders of the day have been called I have heard the hon. member for Lake Centre complain about the kind of answers he has been receiving and ask why he has not been obtaining the information he sought. A check through Hansard will show many occasions on which similar objection has been raised, and I have in mind one in particular which prompts me to speak in this debate.
First of all, I do not know why a question of mine about freight assistance on western feed grains should have been passed as an order for return, because it affected only one department of government. However, a return was brought down on May 16. The questions were as follows:
1.	Is freight assistance on western feed grains granted in Canada beyond Fort William, Ontario, or Vancouver, British Columbia?
2.	If so, where to?
3.	Are milling companies or feed companies permitted freight assistance or drawback on freight on oats or coarse grains purchased or handled by them?
4.	If so, what companies during 1948 and 1949 obtained freight assistance or drawback on coarse grains and what amounts?
I would ask the Minister of Finance if there is anything wrong with that fourth question. The return gave the following reply:
The attached1 information has been received by the Secretary of State of Canada from the Department of Agriculture.
1.	Freight assistance is paid on feed grain shipped from Fort William to all eastern provinces, and from Edmonton and Calgary to points in British Columbia.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
3.	Freight assistance is paid to wholesale handlers of feeds and feed grain on submission of proof that-
(1)	The grain has been shipped and the freight paid.
(2)	That the grain has been sold to a consumer, retail dealer or co-operative and

(3)	That the consumer or retail buyer has been allowed the freight assistance claimed by the wholesaler.
4.	Answered by No. 3.
I will ask the Minister of Finance if he does not agree that in that answer I have been given the run-around. It speaks for itself.
I certainly did not receive information that I asked for very pointedly. But I tell you that in my humble way I have been able to obtain some information myself. There was no reason why that question should not have had a proper answer. These things should be followed up and more information should be given. As we all know, hon. members have been trying to get information on the expenditure of the taxpayer's money.
Just the other day the hon. member whom the Minister of Finance said was an expert on getting information asked some questions in connection with coarse grains. And the fact is that instead of these figures being increased, in a great many instances they could well be reduced because today we have air carriage of mail, which in ordinary cases is almost as fast as service by telephone or telegram.
One of the things that a competent group of independent experts would examine would

be the extent to which just as effective communication could be carried out by the speedy use of air mail as by the use of telephones and telegrams at the present time; and whether there are more departments in Ottawa brought under the Department of Finance, and other departments outside operating separately, makes no difference. These are the figures given by officials of the Department of Finance itself as to the comparative costs. I am not suggesting for one moment that this is not in every way an accurate representation of the figure. On the contrary, I am satisfied that it is. Whatever the balancing may be between departments, the totals have increased enormously.
In so far as the over-all picture is concerned, the items that I have given are only a few of the combined items that show very great increases under headings that certainly are subject to ordinary business examination. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in this case there is no abrogation of the responsibility of parliament by the appointment of a royal commission to go into a subject of this kind. In fact, if that argument is sound then there would be no single case where a royal commission could properly be appointed, because whenever a royal commission is appointed it is for the purpose of examining into some public affairs.
One of the statements made by certain speakers on this amendment is that -this would be a commission of judges. I simply point out that I have suggested that this commission be set up on a basis similar to the commission which was set up in the United States under the chairmanship of ex-president Hoover. Whether there be a judge or judges is of course entirely a matter of responsibility for the government that would be called upon to make the appointments and to set the terms of the reference. I did make it clear that I believed a royal commission of this kind could best carry out its purpose if it were made up of business experts, and of experts in accounting and others who by their training could effectively deal with matters of this kind.
We of course cannot say that the result would be on the same proportionate basis. But it is interesting to note that the Hoover commission in the United States, inquiring into the same general subject, made recommendations which it is estimated would amount to an annual saving of $5 billion. In this country on a proportionate basis it would amount to a saving in excess of $400 million. I am not saying that such a commission could of necessity make recommendations that would bring about a saving of that kind.
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry What I do say is that only a commission of that kind could determine the extent of the savings that could be made. If the savings are $50 million, $100 million, $150 million or $200 million, they are the kind of savings that we want at this time.
In this country, as in other countries, the war necessarily expanded the business of government. I wish that the government itself would accept these arguments without suggesting that we are necessarily imputing any improper handling of the public business when we say that savings could be made. When Mr. Hoover's commission, a large commission, got to work it set up a number of teams, and those teams examined different subjects. I do not recall any suggestion from either side of congress that there was anything unfair about the claim at that time that savings could be made. In fact Mr. Hoover, the ex-president, representing one party, was appointed by the president who belonged to another party, and that very non-political and impartial approach to this subject has been carried right through. All over the United States today public committees, made up of people of the two major parties in the United States, are organized to carry into effect and to obtain the implementation of the recommendations of the Hoover commission.
I should think that the government itself would welcome the opportunity to gain the assistance that it would receive from the constructive examination of departmental organization and accounting procedure by the most competent people who could be called to this service throughout the whole of Canada.
Although opposition has been expressed to this motion, I still urge the government to reconsider the position and to consider the advantage that there will be to the government, as well as to the people of Canada, if the whole organization of government in relation to its public accounting system, and the whole system of public expenditure, be so examined as to ensure that the taxpayer gets as close as possible to one hundred cents value for every dollar that he has to pay.

The questions were passed as orders for returns on April 24. The first question reads as follows:
What was the amount expended month by month since the first of April, 1949, to date in all departments of government for (a) travelling expenses: (b) living expenses and allowances?

. In so far as the delay in giving the answers to those questions is concerned, I do not want to bring it up every day as a question of privilege. subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, April 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, inter alia, to extend the provisions of "Part II-Control of Elevators and Railways" to August 1, 1953; to extend the definition of "pool period" to include each crop year subsequent to July 31, 1950, and prior to August 31, 1953; to vary the payments by the board to producers selling and delivering wheat produced in a designated area; to extend the provisions of "Part TV-Regulation of Interprovincial and Export Trade in Wheat," to August 1, 1953; and to substitute a schedule of mills and warehouses declared works for the.general advantage of Canada for the present schedule to the act.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems a long while since I moved the adjournment of this debate on April 20, after the statement on the introduction of this resolution had been made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Since that time he has been abroad. Today he gave the house a very general statement regarding the outcome of the negotiations that he and the deputy minister had been engaged in in London over a period of several days. It is impossible to discuss in any detail the statement that was made today by the minister, for he himself said that, apart from giving the general outline, the particulars would not be given or furnished to the house at this time.
Even on the basis of the general outline that he has given, the wheat farmers of western Canada will be greatly disappointed at the failure to realize the promises so easily made from 1945 to 1949 of the benefits that would result from their accepting losses

running into at least $600 million over a period of years. In return for acceptance of lower prices then they were promised security. There will be disappointment at the nature of the arrangements that have been arrived at between the minister, on behalf of the people of Canada, and the government of the United Kingdom.
It is a far cry from the sure hopes that were expressed over and over again by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as to the benefits that were to accrue to the Canadian farmer in return for the sacrifices that were made at his expense in selling his wheat under the British agreement at a price of from 75 cents to $1.10 per bushel less than the world market.
We on this side of the house-and this applies to His Majesty's loyal opposition alone-warned what the results would be. I remember well on a number of occasions the then leader of the opposition, Mr. John Bracken, reiterated his view that the course being followed would not give to the Canadian wheat farmer an assured wheat market in the United Kingdom after the termination of the agreement. He was ridiculed for that stand.
He and this party supported the British agreement in so far as selling wheat to Britain was concerned at a price below the world market; but contended that the loss thereby suffered should not be saddled on the back of the wheat farmer, but should be assumed by the people of Canada as a whole. The answer always was in effect "Wait and you shall see. After 1950 there will be an assured wheat market in the United Kingdom." The message brought back today by the Minister of Trade and Commerce is a far cry from the optimistic statements made between 1945 and 1949. Instead of an assured market the minister brings a hope. In place of security he expresses the hope that there will be a market for 110 million bushels or more. That is far from the promises that were made between 1945 and 1949 when the western wheat farmer accepted the low prices that were given him in the agreement in return for the promises made by the ministers of this government that he would be assured of markets after the termination of the agreement.
I shall say no more at this time until the minister elucidates and explains the terms of the negotiations that have taken place. Suffice it to say that after listening to him today disappointment will indeed be expressed, and properly so, by the wheat farmers of this country having regard to the losses they have sustained during the period from 1945 55946-190
Canadian Wheat Board Act to 1949. All they have in return is whatever is provided for under the international wheat agreement.
Apparently there is no compulsory requirement that Britain shall buy any quantity. The only provision is that a large portion of her requirements will be bought in Canada at a price between $1.55 and $1.90, as the minister said today.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext: I said $1.54 and $1.98.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext:
Having said that, and
awaiting further explanations as to the negotiations, I am going to refer to the resolution.
The criticisms that I receive from farmers in connection with this resolution and the wheat board policy are as follows:	First this
resolution, providing for the extension of the pool period to include each crop year subsequent to July 31, 1950, and prior to August 31, 1953, is a continuation almost from year to year of the short term policies that have characterized this government in connection with this matter.
What the farmer objects to is the piecemeal policy. He was promised security not for a year or two but for a considerable period after the expiration of the 1950 period in the British agreements.
The farmer expects a guaranteed market. That is what he was promised. He now feels -and he will feel this more strongly when he reads the announcement that the minister has made-that the sacrifices he endured under the British agreement have indeed been in vain, and that now he has no real guarantee of security. He has the international agreement which is full of the loopholes which were inserted in order to arrive at agreement.
The farmer is asking for a long term policy for wheat marketing, not the piecemeal policy that is being followed now, which is immeasurably deficient when compared with the promises that were made during the period from 1945 to 1949.
Secondly, farmers cannot understand-and this applies particularly in the drought areas of the prairie provinces-why there was a denial on the part of the government and of the wheat board of an interim wheat payment this year. It could have been made applicable to those areas in the prairie provinces subject to drought. There was nothing to prevent it, including the bookkeeping difficulties alleged as an excuse by the government. The farmers are commencing to wonder whether the reason there was no interim payment is that there is little or nothing to the credit of the farmers available for final distribution, much less available for interim payment.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
Thirdly, the farmers believe they have the right to expect that the business of the wheat board shall be submitted to the committee on agriculture. We have not had such a submission to that committee for two and a half years. Why? This is one board, one crown corporation, or emanation of the crown, that is not subject to examination by the Auditor General.
Surely the report should be placed before the committee on agriculture to the end that questions may be asked, and accounts in connection with its mammoth transactions be subjected to examination and cross-examination. When we endeavour to get information in parliament, as the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) said today, we have difficulty in getting answers. If we try to get information respecting the wheat board and its transactions we are invariably met by a curtain that denies any information sought and the house is denied the opportunity of examining wheat board accounts in the committee on agriculture.

speechtext:
He was asked by the hon. member for Souris this year to submit it to the committee, and was asked by him and by other hon. members last year. And I now repeat the request, if the Minister of Trade and Commerce has not heard it previously, that the report be submitted, so that examination may be made of the accounts.
We cannot get the information in parliament. No department is more difficult to penetrate for information than is the Department of Trade and Commerce. I asked this question on May 22:
1.	How many bushels of (a) feed oats; (b) feed barley, were sold by the wheat board to feed merchants, dealers or brokerage houses in each of the months beginning in December, 1949 and to date?
What was the purpose of that question? Surely the farmers in this country have a right to the information there sought, because in the main they are the producers. The farmers in western Canada are asking what has happened to the barley and oats they produced. Is it a fact that the wheat board has sold a large portion of it to brokerage firms in the United States? They would like to have answers to it and other questions.
The farmers in eastern Canada who feed cattle and hogs want to know why the prices of barley and oats are so high. They want to know what has happened to feed supplies. They want to know whether or not the wheat board has made any provision for the sale of feed oats and barley to eastern farmers engaged in livestock production.
The next question is:
2.	What was the average price received for each of said grains in each of said months?
Eighty per cent of our coarse grain production is fed or disposed of in Canada. What possible harm could there be in furnishing that information? When the people of Canada ask for information, when the farmers in western Canada and in Ontario ask for information, the answer given by the government is:
It is not the policy of the Canadian wheat board to divulge its sales position within the crop year in which it is operating.
I am not going to deny that position as far as wheat on the international market is concerned, but that argument does not apply to sales of barley and oats within Canada, commodities that are so necessary to the eastern farmer and eastern livestock producer for feeding purposes. The Minister of Finance has said in effect: "Ask and the information 55946-1904
Canadian Wheat Board Act will be given." Yet when a simple question such as that is asked, the farmers, the producers of livestock and the producers of barley and oats witness a brush-off of parliament, a denial by the wheat board of information to which parliament is entitled.
If the wheat board report is submitted to the committee an opportunity will be given to ask these questions and receive the information denied to parliament. I ask what recourse the opposition has against an allpowerful government supported by an allpowerful majority when information is denied regardless of whether or not it is justifiable. Up until recent years information could be denied by a minister of the crown only on the ground that it was not in the public interest, but that has been extended. Three members of the wheat board are able to say to parliament in effect "We just do not choose to answer; that is not a course that we are going to follow, the giving of information within the crop year in which we are operating".
This is the first year in which the wheat board has the exclusive marketing control of barley and oats and there have been difficulties. The western farmer is asking whether the wheat board has disposed of his oats and barley elsewhere than in Canada. He wants to know what prices have been received and whether or not the wheat board in effect is discharging its responsibility of getting the best price for oats and barley rather than doing what it did under the British agreements-secure a political price determined by the government rather than by world demand.
The members of the Progressive Conservative party believe that the farmers should have some say in the marketing of their own products. We have fought for the principle that the producers should have some control over the marketing of their wheat, oats and barley. We believe in the necessity-we think the events of the last few years support-us in this regard-of an advisory board made up of a majority of farmers being set up to advise the wheat board to the end that the best possible prices may be received and so the farm producer will have some say as to the disposal of his wheat, oats and barley. The board should be a producers' wheat board operating for the benefit of the farmers in accordance with business principles.
For the past five years wheat farmers have been deluded by the promise that for the sacrifice of several hundred millions of dollars in prices that could have been secured for their wheat they were to have security of market after the termination of

Canadian Wheat Board Act the British agreement in 1950. The statement made by the minister today is an effective answer to any who were minded to suffer from such a delusion.
The minister's statement occupies but two pages of Hansard. It states that discussions have been carried on in London and that both governments have now reviewed the results of those talks and are agreed that the international wheat agreement removes the need for a contract to replace the existing Anglo-Canadian wheat agreement. That was not the view one year ago. That was not the view six months ago. That was not the view expressed during the campaign just prior to the last election.
Finally the minister said, in summary, that the United Kingdom has made it clear that out of its total wheat import requirements in 1950-51, it expects to buy a large proportion in Canada which, quite apart from the special contractual arrangements for the past four years, is, and it is hoped will remain, the traditional source of supply for the United Kingdom. The minister's speech was an expression of hope, when instead he should have given parliament evidence of the security that was promised during the period of the British agreements.
With these few observations I will conclude. I believe the announcement made by the minister will be received with deep disappointment by wheat farmers, for it fails to carry out the promises made so clearly over five long years that the farmers of western Canada would achieve security after the termination of the agreements in return for the sale of their wheat at prices below world prices. What many farmers are thinking is indicated by a resolution recently sent to me by the Quinton wheat pool committee which reads as follows:
That we the Quinton wheat pool committee feel that our M.P. should back up the resolution of the federation of agriculture, that the farmer be reimbursed1 through the wheat board for the subsidizing of wheat used for home consumption during part of the five-year pool.
That indicates that by reason of the failure of this government and the wheat board to provide the security that was promised, farmers throughout the west are beginning to ask that they be reimbursed for the losses they have suffered in subsidizing wheat used for home consumption.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

I will take only a few minutes to
do that, for I am glad that the house is prepared to vote on this measure. As I indicated in moving the second reading of the bill, its purpose is very clear and direct. It asks for the voluntary revocable check-off of trade union dues. It proposes that the check-off shall be brought into effect only when asked for by a union certified under this act; and even then it is to apply only in the case of those employees who request in writing that the check-off for their dues be made from their wages. It is also clear from the provisions of the act that if any of those employees later request that the check-off cease, it shall cease forthwith.
As I indicated in introducing this measure, it is a move for which there is recorded support on the part of all political parties in this house. All parties indicated during the course of the last election campaign that they favoured various measures of union security. This, as I have pointed out, is the minimum measure of union security; that is, the voluntary revocable check-off of union dues. I also indicated the last time I spoke on this measure that the wording of the bill now before the house, as far as this new section which would be written into the bill is concerned, is precisely the same as the wording that was put in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act when that measure was reported back to this house by the industrial relations committee in 1948. On that occasion the bill, after second reading, was referred to the industrial relations committee without this clause in it; but during the deliberations of that committee this clause was written in on the motion of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). As I have already pointed out, the wording proposed in the first instance by the hon. member was later revised at the suggestion of the legal adviser of the Department of Labour. I am not thereby suggesting that the legal adviser necessarily supported the principle of the proposal; but at least, that principle having been endorsed by the committee, it was then put in a form acceptable to the legal adviser.
The bill that came back to the house in 1948, therefore, contained-word for word-this very clause which my bill seeks to write into the labour code. Here on the floor of the house during discussion of the bill clause by
Industrial Relations
clause, on the motion of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Little), that clause was dropped out of the labour code. I feel the time has now come when it should be put back in, and I think it well that the house should have had this chance to consider the matter over two or three of these private members' hours. When the vote is called I hope members of all parties will stand by the position they have taken, particularly during election campaigns, by endorsing this minimum measure of union security.

If that is so, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word or two on this legislation. I am not in favour of the bill, and I put it on rather broad grounds. This house has already defeated similar measures on the same grounds that I now bring before the house. I refer to the whole
Industrial Relations
scheme of the act respecting industrial relations, on which some of us at the last session and the one before spent a great deal of time. I think the committee are to be congratulated on bringing out a piece of legislation which received almost the unanimous support of the house. I agree with the argument, which has been used in connection with other measures, that a bill passed with general approbation should be allowed some time to operate without, from year to year, submitting amendments to bring about some result which, in size, is very limited when compared with those broad things accomplished by the bill itself.
The principle behind this measure is one involving judgment in a dispute. It involves the enforcing of judgments by bodies other than those courts which, in the experience of all of us, in times past, have been the custodian of that authority. The bill is brief, and gives to the board the right to fix compensation for persons who have been discharged contrary to the provisions of the act.
My main point is that if someone has done something to someone else and, in doing so, has acted contrary to law, then our courts have always been open and, indeed, are now open, to give that person redress against the wrongdoer. He who is in breach of the law is always the wrongdoer. Without commenting at all on hurry-up methods of dealing with legal matters I content myself with saying just this, that past experience has shown us that when we seek shortcuts we usually get ourselves into more difficulties than we would have had if we had followed the normal, orderly and ordinary procedure.
It may be that the sponsors and advocates of this measure have in mind the case of a discharged person who has felt he was not treated fairly. All of us at times have felt that way. But after all in this country there are courts who are charged with, accept and discharge the responsibility of deciding whether we as individuals have in fact been treated fairly.
This bill seeks to give a board the right to say that so-and-so was treated unfairly, and that therefore compensation as provided by the board should be paid to the aggrieved person. My point is that if a person, to use the language of the bill, has been discharged contrary to the provisions of the act, such person has suffered-and I hesitate to use legal language-a tort, or a wrongdoing. Who is there to suggest that our courts are not competent to take care of any proper claim that a tort has been done against an individual?
In short the bill states that-
The board shall have power to make an order requiring an employer to reinstate any employee

Industrial Relations
discharged contrary to the provisions of this act and to pay such employee the monetary loss suffered by reason of such discharge.
I do not complain very much about the language. But when I see people bringing into this House of Commons bills which are onesided, then I am opposed to them. If the hon. member had said that in the event of an employee doing something by way of injury to his employer such employer should seek equal rights before the board as against the employee, then perhaps I could see at least some fairness and some moral soundness in the idea behind the advancement of this bill. But this business of special legislation and special pleading for the friends of any group in the house must come to naught, unless they are broad enough to be fair to all parties concerned.
I fall back to my original statement, and that is to say that I am aware of criticisms of our courts; I know they are not perfect. I also know that no man-made thing has ever been perfect, and that perhaps such will never be perfect. But I do say this, with some knowledge of my subject, that in so far as we in the House of Commons believe in the administration of justice-and that is what this is- by our courts, we accept it as the best system yet found by any civilized people since the world began.
So I say the minute we start whittling and chiselling at the jurisdiction of our courts, to effect some special thing we have in mind- a _ single-track mind, if you like-at that minute we begin cutting down the jurisdiction of our courts, and immediately find ourselves in trouble.
It may be that the hon. member has something in mind. Perhaps I should modify that statement, because I know he has a great deal in his mind. My meaning was that it may be that he thinks there are some evils that are so general they should be dealt with by legislation in parliament. If that were true I would have a great deal of sympathy, and certainly have an open mind as to how I might vote in respect of a proposal of that kind. But I would need to be convinced that our courts had failed in their bounden duty, that the scales of justice had not been held evenly-which I do not for one moment believe. I would need to be convinced that there was some broad and general difficulty which would prompt parliament to enter into a field of legislation which would take care of some narrow business and which procedure in the end might not result in any good but rather in evil toward the whole structure.
I am opposed to the bill. I go a step further, and in making this statement I know I

am not going to popularize myself with the voters. I wonder if we appreciate that labour today owes its very high position to legislation passed by parliaments and legislatures. I wonder how much the sponsor of this bill appreciates the simple fact that the growth of union organizations since the last war has been tremendous-and, so far as I am concerned, rightly so. I wonder if we all appreciate the tremendous gains which have been made. Why have they been made? They have been made because parliaments, congresses, legislatures, United Kingdom parliaments and so on have said two things: first, that no labour organization may be held liable in a charge of conspiracy. That is the thing upon which it is all founded. We have also said that the treasury

I will admit that there has been an alteration in the United States under the recent legislation-of a labour organization shall be free and exempt from civil action against the organization. I agree with both those things. I think they are the foundation upon which this tremendous growth has been built. But I say to all of these people: Do not work a willing horse to death.
They have made great progress. I have acted for them and I know something about them. I am not one of those who, every time the name of John Lewis is mentioned, use an expression which is quite unparliamentary. I am not blind to the tremendous service which that man has rendered labour on the North American continent. I remember the situation in the coal mines in many places in the United States and even in Canada where there were company houses and company stores and everybody owed the employer money at the end of the month.
Do not let us get personal about this thing and condemn somebody because he has committed excesses. Labour has committed excesses, but so has capital, and lots of them. I think the great thing that has been achieved by thinking people in the Dominion of Canada is that no longer shall industry regard labour as simply an intake product in the factory. A great gain has been made in that connection. With the assistance of the minister and other like-minded people the growth of labour has been tremendous. All we need to do is look at the settlement of that great automobile strike the other day. That would have been utterly impossible a few weeks ago. I am not going to talk out this motion, but I cannot say that I am going to vote against it because my pair is not here. But at least I am making my sentiments known.
I am going to give some advice to my hon. friends who sit to my left. I cannot charge them for it and they would not pay me

if I did. Why not leave well enough alone? Why not flex your muscles and appreciate the wonderful growth you have had? But do not try to rush the growler too hard.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe that the house go into committee on the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, inter alia, to extend the provisions of "Part II-Control of Elevators and Railways" to August 1, 1953; to extend the definition of "pool period" to include each crop year subsequent to July 31, 1950, and-prior to August 31, 1953; to vary the payments by the board to producers selling and delivering wheat produced in a designated area; to extend the provisions of "Part IV-Regulation of Interprovincial and Export Trade in Wheat," to August 1, 1953; and to substitute a schedule of mills and warehouses declared works for the general advantage of Canada for the present schedule to the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext:
I have here an index, published by the dominion bureau of statistics, which sets forth the index for eleven important commodities going into the farmers' costs of production. That index is based on 1935-39 equals 100. The eleven commodities include farm implements, building material, gasoline, oil, grease, feed, fertilizer, binder twine, seed, hardware, tax rates, interest rates and farm wages; in other words, almost all of the important costs of production that the farmer must meet. In January of this year that index was 196-3, or almost twice as much as it was in 1935-39. And so you have the initial price for wheat for the coming year roughly twice that of the initial price in the immediate pre-war period. You have the farmer's costs of production twice as high, so that the farmer, in my opinion, is going back to the pre-war depression subsistence level. Therefore I say without question that within the last few months and the last few weeks and again today the farmers of western Canada have had levelled against them a number of serious blows resulting from the changes in the government's wheat policy.
There are to be no further large initial payments this spring. There is to be a drop of 35 cents a bushel in the initial price on August 1 of this year. There is to be a floor price for only one year at a time. No longer will there be long-term stability. Then there was the announcement by the minister this afternoon that we are going to take a reduction, according to his estimation, of not less than 20 million bushels in the quantity of wheat that we will ship to the United Kingdom this year, and if his lower figure proves the correct one it will be a reduction of 40 million bushels.
I say it is time the government reconsidered its policy, in the light of the sacrifices that our producers have made over the last number of years, when they accepted prices we all knew were below world prices, and were below the prices that could have been obtained from the domestic consumer if prices for agricultural products, as was done in everything else, had been allowed to find their own level.
Instead, the government said: We are going to give you a price stabilization policy; we say to you that we are not going to let you have the highest possible price, but when prices start to fall we are not going to ask you to take the lowest price. The farmer said: I agree that that is a good policy, and even if I make great sacrifices over a few years, I know that I shall have a chance to recoup my losses.

It has been estimated by various members how much the farmer has lost. I do not think anyone will ever know precisely but it runs into hundreds of millions of dollars. We know that the floor price under the international wheat agreement for the coming year is $1.54 in Canadian funds; yet we have the government setting an initial price 14 cents a bushel below the floor price in the international agreement, and that may well be all the farmer will get; I do not know.
Before Easter the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) explained why that might be all he would get. At the end of the 1950-51 crop year the wheat board would very likely have a considerable carryover of wheat that would have to be marketed in the first months of the next year, being a year when the floor price under the international agreement fell another 10 cents a bushel. The government is therefore playing it safe. They are not risking anything in their present legislation. But the result of a drop of 35 cents a bushel in the initial price for wheat, a further loss of our international markets for wheat, along with the loss of a great many other markets for agricultural products, may spell such a substantial reduction in the standard of living in western Canada that it will affect all of the people from one coast of this country to the other.
I think we are getting in a vicious circle. The government adopts certain policies from time to time. We have no industries in western Canada. We have a policy adopted like this one that will mean a lowering of our economic standard. Then we have an exodus of people and we lose some of our seats in the House of Commons. Everyone who sits in this house knows that if any part of Canada wants to get a square deal it has to have an effective voice in parliament. When you lose population you lose seats; and when you lose seats you lose influence with the government of the day. Then when we do have some natural resources like oil in Alberta the first thing the government arranges is to take it out of that area to other parts of Canada and the United States.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the government should reconsider its wheat policy. If the present wheat policy is adopted, if nothing is done to arrest the losing of our agricultural markets, all the government will succeed in doing is to establish a depressed area on the prairies, the same kind of depressed area we had before the war. In my opinion, if that should result, it will certainly not be in the
Canadian Wheat Board Act best interests of Canada, and the government should adopt a wheat policy so that such a condition will not obtain.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am going to be quite brief in my remarks. There are a number of questions that I want to raise but I shall leave them until we get into the committee stage of the resolution.
We in this group support the resolution because we are of the opinion that it is in the interests of the people of Canada, and more especially in the interests of the grain growers of Canada, that the wheat board continue to operate as a hundred per cent marketing agency for all wheat grown in Canada. Moreover we believe that the permit book and quota system is the fairest way of handling deliveries of grain in western Canada. It always amuses me when I hear people commiserating with the farmers for being compelled to sell their wheat to the wheat board, instead of being allowed to choose what market they want, because I have always found that ninety-nine times out of a hundred these people are not farmers and are far more concerned about the welfare of the grain trade and the grain exchange than about the welfare of the farmers.
I always feel that if the day should come when we make the selling of wheat optional, and permit the decision whether it be sold to the wheat board or on the open market, we shall have signed the death warrant of the wheat board. Furthermore I am satisfied that an overwhelming majority of farmers in western Canada are solidly behind the wheat board today, and in my view the personnel of that board is to be highly commended for the efficient way it has handled the farmers' wheat in the past.
It is true that we hear many people criticize the wheat board on the ground that they lost money for the farmers by subsidizing the British consumer and the Canadian consumer during the time of the British wheat agreement. It is unquestionably true that the farmers did suffer heavy losses as a result of that action. But the mistake these people make is that they blame the wheat board for that situation, instead of the government. That action, of course, was forced upon the wheat board by the government. That is to say, the wheat board was forced to sell wheat to Great Britain below the current market price as a result of the government's having signed the British wheat agreement. They were forced to sell wheat to Canadian millers at less than current prices as a result of orders in council passed 1 believe under the War Measures Act.
We in this group take the very definite stand that the government should not use the

Canadian Wheat Board Act wheat board as an instrument of government policy to limit domestic prices or to subsidize foreign countries. If it is government policy to subsidize Canadian consumers or the consumers in foreign countries by giving them cheap wheat, then let them buy the wheat from the wheat board at current prices, sell it at whatever price they see fit, and then absorb the loss resulting from such action.
That has been the stand taken by farm organizations. For instance, let me quote from a resolution passed by the western agricultural conference held at Saskatoon, January 20 to 22, 1949. It states:
That the Canadian wheat board should be an agency operating in the interests of grain producers, with a duty at all times to sell grain for the best available price whether in export or domestic markets, and should not be used as an instrument of government policy to limit domestic prices.
It is well to remember that parliament was' *asked to support the British wheat agreement in part at least as a moral obligation. I recall only too well the discussion which took place *at that time, when it was pointed out that [DOT]Great Britain had made great sacrifices and that therefore we should be willing to help her out by allowing her to have wheat at a reasonable price. The House of Commons was glad to support the British wheat agreement on that basis, but many of us in the opposition of that day pointed out that if it was a moral obligation on the part of the Canadian people to allow Britain to have wheat at reduced prices, then it was the moral responsibility of the Canadian people to stand whatever loss resulted from allowing Britain to have wheat at those reduced prices.
The same thing of course applies in connection with selling wheat to millers at less than the price of No. II wheat. Not only did we let millers have wheat below the price of No. II class wheat but actually we allowed them to have it for less than the price we charged under the British wheat agreement in 1946 and 1947.
Before the bill passes the minister should indicate the government's policy in regard to compensating farmers for these losses resulting from government action. I am not asking the minister to say what the amount of the final payment of the five-year pool will be, but merely to give the assurance that some at least of the losses will be made up in that payment.
I recall that during the last session of the last parliament, in the concluding days, the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) asked the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) what the government policy would be in
[Mr. Quelch.I

regard to meeting these losses. Hansard for April 30, 1949, at page 2802 contains the following question by the hon. member:
X should like to ask the Prime Minister a question. Is it the intention of the present government, if returned to office after the coming election, to reimburse the farmers of the prairie provinces for the losses which they have sustained under the wheat agreements?
The Prime Minister replied:
I do not think it would be proper for any party to be making promises at this time as to what it will do. I am sure that whatever government is in office at that time will endeavour to reach a decision that will be fair both to the farmers and to the Canadian public generally.
Of course I know some people might say that does not mean very much. But after all when a statement of that kind is made by the Prime Minister I suggest it should mean a great deal. It should mean that the government intends to do the right thing or the fair thing by the farmers in meeting these losses. The wheat pools are suggesting that a 25-cent payment should be made. This of course would by no means cover the total losses, but on the other hand it would compensate for approximately half of the losses incurred during that time; and the balance of that loss could be made up by stabilizing the price of wheat in the future.
It is all very well for the minister to say that the farmers have had better returns in the past five years than in any former period. I would not dispute that for one moment. But at the same time farmers' costs have also been higher in those five years than during any other period; and today while the prices farmers are receiving for their produce are beginning to fall, their costs are still rising.
Let us not forget that in those years before the war farmers were taking very low prices for their produce and were told time and again that they could not expect to receive more than the world market price. So they hoped that when prices went up they would have a chance to recover some of their losses. Yet when the war came and prices went up to a high level the government set ceilings and farmers were not allowed to receive world market prices. It does seem only natural that if in peacetime farmers are told that they must be satisfied with world market prices, then in wartime when prices go up they should be allowed to receive the full benefit of those increased prices. But the ceiling was maintained in the name of stabilization and therefore the government have a definite obligation to stabilize prices in the future and thus fulfil their part of the bargain.
I find it hard to understand why the government considered it necessary to set the initial payment for the next crop year at $1.40 per bushel, 14 cents below the floor

price under the international wheat agreement. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) prides himself upon being an optimist and he always tells us on this side that we are pessimistic, but it seems to me that he is taking a pessimistic view of the operations of the international wheat agreement when he finds it necessary to set a price 14 cents below the floor in that agreement. It does not look as though he has much confidence in the international wheat agreement. Although that agreement provides for a fluctuation from $1.54 to $1.98 the minister is not satisfied to keep the Canadian initial payment within those limits; he has placed it 14 cents below the floor established by the international wheat agreement.
If the government feared that by setting the initial payment at $1.54 per bushel some losses might be incurred, they should remember that over the past eight years or so the prices of farm products have been kept down in the name of stabilization. If any losses were suffered as a result of setting a price of $1.54 that would only be helping to stabilize prices as they promised to do during the years when the ceiling was maintained.
We in this group supported the international wheat agreement. If the international wheat agreement fails, in my opinion it will not be because the idea of long-term international wheat agreements is not sound; it will be because of the system of financing international trade that exists. Under the agreement, if a nation is unable to purchase its quota it can be released from its obligation. It will be our responsibility to see that we purchase enough goods from a nation to enable it to buy wheat from us. The international commodity clearing house would have provided a means by which we could have disposed of our surpluses. The government stated at that time that they were in a position to look after their own surpluses so the problem is definitely on the doorstep of the government. I certainly hope that they will not fail in the handling of our wheat problem and I repeat that if the international wheat agreement fails it will be largely oecause of certain international financial and trade policies that are being followed.
Fear is being expressed regarding possible surpluses of wheat in the future, but if you go through history you will find that we have never really had too much wheat. Wheat has accumulated in some years, but over a period of time those surpluses have all disappeared. It is largely a question of providing sufficient storage to carry the surpluses over from one year to another. When you look at the
Canadian Wheat Board Act situation in the world today, when you consider the position of China, India and other countries, you can feel assured that there will be adequate markets for all the wheat we can raise, provided we make satisfactory trading agreements whereby nations can obtain our wheat.

speechtext:
In this case the greatest speculators have been the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). They made a terrific gamble when they entered into a contract with Great Britain to deliver six hundred million bushels of wheat over a four-year period, when that wheat had not even been seeded. If anyone ever made a greater gamble in the marketing of wheat I should like to hear about it.
This is the first year the government has had a monopoly of the handling of oats and barley through the Canadian wheat board. In spite of the fact, as has been pointed out by various ministers, that it is not customary to give the trading position throughout the year, I believe we should have that information before we pass the new bill. I am bound to agree with the hon. member who preceded

me that the majority of the people in the west want to deal through the wheat board, but they do not want a political board; they want producer representation. Many of those same people in my neighbourhood, and I think other hon. members will say the same thing, are very dubious about the marketing of their coarse grains this year. I do not sell coarse grains; I buy them from my neighbours and feed the grains on my farm, and I am not sure whether I have been doing that legally for the past year. My neighbours selling grain at the elevator have been paid for good oats only 52 cents a bushel. Mind you, that does not include the freight to Fort William, but their price at the local elevator is 52 cents. In the estimate given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to further payments at the end of the year-and I agree that it was only an estimate-he said they might get 10 cents a bushel. That would give them a total of 62 cents, if his estimate were right. I have before me a speech delivered by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Gour) just outside Ottawa, pointing out that No. 3 C.W. oats were selling at $76 per ton at stations in that neighbourhood, less a subsidy of $6 per ton. A little arithmetic will tell you that this amounts to something like $1.45 a bushel in sacks less the subsidy. You cannot tell me there is that much difference in cost; so I say those farmers are very dubious. I am not making any charge as to where the great difference arises; I am citing this as a logical reason why we should be able to question the officials of the board on the handling of coarse grains before we pass a new bill after this experiment.
At this stage, as I say, I do not wish to take a great deal of time. I am one of those who cannot see why the floor price on wheat, or to be more factual the initial payment, should be only $1.40, when the international agreement provides that for this year the minimum price will be $1.54 and the maximum price $1.98. Surely if the government had faith in that deal they should be able to pay more than $1.40 as a minimum, and I believe that requires some explanation as well.
You know, Mr. Speaker, it is rather strange how things can change in a few months. I have before me a copy of the Winnipeg Free Press of June 15, 1949, where I see a heading, "Would hurt farmer. Howe scores mention of devaluing dollar." By the way, the minister was addressing a meeting at Portage la Prairie that day, and as quoted in this article he said:
If the dollar were devalued, he said, it would assist certain branches of the gold mining industry ''because the price of gold would be increased by
Canadian Wheat Board Act the percentage that the dollar is devalued." But other sections of the Canadian public, he emphasized, would suffer.
For example, if the dollar were devalued by ten per cent it would mean that the western farmer under the wheat agreement with the United Kingdom would get ten per cent less in net return for every bushel sold and conversely, the cost of living for consumers would go up by ten per cent as Canadians would be required to pay for imports from the United States with a depreciated dollar.
"We have seen what happens in other countries when they try working with a depreciated dollar," he remarked, "and I believe no one is so foolish as to think that a step of this kind is required or wise under present conditions in Canada."
Oddly enough in the same edition of this newspaper there is a press report of a speech by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) at Montreal on the same date, in which he said how silly devaluation would be. There is also a report in the same issue of an address by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) at Minnedosa, in which he discussed the very same topic. That was on June 15. We all know what happened on September 19, when we had devaluation by this government. If the statement made on that occasion by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was true, by that step the government added to that extent to the difficulties we prophesied the farmers were headed for under that contract.
I hope this government will give very serious consideration to reimbursing these farmers at least to some extent. I know they will not expect 100 cents on the dollar for all they have contributed to the consumers of both Great Britain and Canada, but I can tell you that resolutions have been passed by farm organizations of the west asking for a settlement on the basis of at least $2 a bushel. If that were done I believe it would cost the federal treasury approximately half the amount of the loss I mentioned earlier. Again I want to appeal to the minister to see that the report of the wheat board is referred to the committee on agriculture, and that the bill which will follow this resolution is also referred to that committee for consideration. I should like to make a few remarks before the resolution is carried. I shall be brief, because I do not want to repeat the arguments that have been advanced by previous speakers. I do want to support the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) and the other hon. members who have asked that this legislation be referred to the committee on agriculture together with the last three annual reports of the Canadian wheat board. I believe that should be done.
While indicating my support for this legislation, I do so with certain reservations. I am
3020	HOUSE OF
Canadian Wheat Board Act convinced that this should not be temporary legislation that we must pass to cover one period after another.
Under this resolution we are extending the definition of the pool period to include each crop year subsequent to July 31, 1950, and extending the provisions of part IV, the regulations for interprovincial and export trade to August 1, 1953. In other words, this government is indicating to the farmers of western Canada that this is temporary legislation. We are just passing it for a period of time, and it is hoped to get rid of it. The wheat producers of western Canada believe in the wheat board. They believe in this wheat board act. They believe it is good legislation, and they would like to see it made permanent legislation by this parliament, not just temporary legislation. The farmers have had sufficient experience of temporary legislation.
During the war there was the War Measures Act, and later the Agricultural Products Marketing Act which was extended from year to year to enable our products to be marketed under the British contracts. Bacon and other products were marketed under that act, with what result? This year our markets and the act are going up in smoke, and we are not likely to have them another year.
