I am quite prepared to send the bill to the committee, but I suggest that the nature of the amendments is such that they could very well be disposed of in committee of the whole. I hope that will carry the judgment of the house as far as the provisions of the bill are concerned.
Some comment has been made on the announcement made today. The idea has been advanced that this is a let-down, a complete let-down in what we could expect in the marketing of wheat. That is not my feeling; that is not the feeling of the wheat board. We are very glad to know that we have a sure sale for more than half of Canada's normal exportable surplus. We have a sale to a market that has been ours for a great many years.
Hon members may ask, what is remarkable about that? Why should not we have that? The situation is this. If the United Kingdom buy the North American supply of wheat from Canada they have to pay cold hard dollars for it. If they purchase the same supply from the United States they do it under Marshall aid, which is not a drain on the United Kingdom dollar situation. Does anyone say that the assurance that they are going to buy these supplies from Canada is not a very valuable concession? I may say that when I got that far in the discussion I was quite ready to come home. We can accept too that we have a sure market for that proportion of Canada's export wheat.
Some say that there is no agreement as to price. Well we have an agreement as to price. We have an international wheat agreement that was made by the government, assisted by a very strong committee of producers. We bad representatives of the three pools, representatives of the United Grain Growers, representatives of the individual farmers. They were unanimous in recommending that agreement to the Canadian government, and the Canadian government was unanimous in believing that that agreement did give security to the farmers of Canada.
In my opinion one agreement at a time is about all we can handle. Last year we had two agreements. The reason was that the international wheat agreement overlapped the period of the bilateral United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement. Next year wheat will be marketed under the international wheat agreement that provides for a maximum price of $1.98 a bushel and a minimum price of $1.54 a bushel. Under the international wheat agreement Canada will receive the North American price. I am

optimistic enough to believe that the price, under the conditions which I think may prevail in the next marketing year, will be at or near the maximum price. Someone who is pessimistic may take the opposite view and say that it will be at or near the minimum price. However, it will be within the terms of the international wheat agreement, and that under present circumstances is about all that I think we should attempt to do about price at this time.
Ordinarily it is considered gambling to make a short sale of wheat, and we will remember that we are talking about the sale of wheat that is not even planted yet. I think we are much safer in allowing the normal law of marketing to prevail now that we are getting away from the abnormal situation of the reconstruction period, and that is what we intend to do then within the limits of the wheat agreement.
Something has been said about an initial payment. As I said, we are getting back to more normal practice and, in setting the initial payment at $1.40, we are following normal and sound pooling practice. The practice for the prosperous years of the pool, or the successful years of the pool, was to set the initial price at 60 per cent of the price of cash wheat in the month of July. That practice was followed in 1923, when the first pool was organized in Alberta, and in 1924, 1925, 1926, 1927 and 1928.
It was not followed in setting the price in 1929. The price was set well above the 60 per cent of the cash wheat price of that day. What happened? Pools went bankrupt, and some of them have not yet finished paying off debts they incurred as a result of having set that initial payment too high. However, that debt was taken over by the provincial governments, and the pools were allowed to pay off the debt over a period.
What happened in 1930? Again, the 1930 initial price was set well above the 60 per cent of the cash wheat price for July of that year. The initial payment was set at $1, and within a month or two it was reduced to 90 cents. The federal government of that day took over at that time, and Mr. McFarland handled the liquidation of that pool for the account of the federal government, with results that farmers in the western provinces are not too anxious to remember.

Canadian Wheat Board Act hon. member for Farkdale, who made himself so popular with his colleagues that he resigned his seat in the House of Commons two or three months later.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext:
That is hardly true, either.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext: Are we going to accept sterling in payment for wheat?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext: All wheat has been and will be paid for in Canadian dollars.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext: From what I heard over the radio tonight, the wheat would be paid for in sterling which would be used to buy British goods which, in reality, would be paid for with the wheat we are selling to Great Britain. As a matter of fact, in a sense that is pretty much what is done. We get British goods. Our wheat is priced here in dollars, and their goods on the other side of the Atlantic are priced in pounds. After all, we are using terms that are a bit confusing, because we speak of our receipts in dollars while they speak of their exports in pounds.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext: We pay for anything we buy from Britain with dollars and they pay us for anything they buy from us in dollars. This is a dollar country.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext: The British company does not receive dollars.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext: No, the dollars are held in Canada. He is paid in pounds by his own government.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext: At what price will wheat be sold to Canadian millers during 1950-51? Will it be the same iprice as in the international wheat agreement?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext: I think that has not been considered, but I would expect that to be so.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext:
In view of the statement made by the minister that there was a vote on that United Kingdom-Canadian wheat agreement, a statement which has been made several times in other debates, I must point out that the minister has never produced Hansard to show that vote. I will help him to clear it up. That agreement was

announced by the previous minister of trade and commerce on July 26, 1946, I believe it was, and there was no opportunity even to debate it until the minister's estimates were brought down later. The vote to which he refers, I suggest, was in connection with amending the Canadian Wheat Board Act in 1947.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext: To make the agreement possible.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL OF ELEVATORS AND RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext:
True, to fulfil the contract, a year later. But there never yet has been a vote on the agreement as such.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Mr. Howe thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 252, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
